Minimum Risk Point Estimation of the Standardized Mean Difference

Source: R/seq_mr_smd.R
seq_mr_smd.Rd

Given the data collected so far from two independent groups, evaluates the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) stopping rule of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) for the standardized mean difference \(\delta = (\mu_1 - \mu_2)/\sigma\). The procedure is for a study in which each observation costs money and a less accurate estimate also has a cost: it stops sampling when the estimated total of the two is as small as it can be. It targets a risk, not a confidence interval, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_mr_smd(group_1, group_2, A, c, gamma = 0.49, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

group_1, group_2

Numeric vectors: the observations collected so far in the first and the second group, at least four in each. Four is the smallest pilot size the article allows, and seq_mr_smd_pilot never returns less.

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of squared estimation error, in the same currency as c. The article builds it as the amount one is willing to pay to estimate the standardized mean difference to within \(\epsilon\), divided by \(\epsilon^2\) (for example \(2500 / 0.5^2 = 10000\)). A single positive number.

c

The cost of sampling one observation: a single positive number when an observation costs the same in both groups, or two positive numbers, c(c1, c2), the cost in group 1 and the cost in group 2, in that order. Either group may be the costlier one.

gamma

The tuning constant of the correction term, strictly between 0 and 1/2; default 0.49. Use the same value as in seq_mr_smd_pilot.

na.rm

Should missing values be removed before the computation? TRUE (the default) removes them; FALSE stops with an error if any are present.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and one row for each of

smd

the standardized mean difference, group 1 minus group 2, divided by the pooled standard deviation;

risk

the approximate risk (Equation 9, or Equation 17 with two costs) at the current group sizes, with the estimate in place of \(\delta\);

mean_1, mean_2

the two sample means;

optimal_n1, optimal_n2

the criterion sample size for each group. With one cost both equal the right side of Equation 15, rounded up. With two costs, the less costly group's value is the right side of its stopping rule, rounded up, and the costlier group's value is the size the article pairs with the larger of the less costly group's current size and its criterion. The rule is met exactly when each current size is at least its criterion;

current_n1, current_n2

the number of observations supplied in each group;

next_n1, next_n2

the size each group should have at the next check. When the rule is met they equal the current sizes: nothing more is called for. Otherwise, with one cost, each group is brought up to one more than the smaller current size. With two costs the less costly group gets one more observation and the costlier group is brought up to the size the article pairs with the less costly group's new size; but if the costlier group is short of the size paired with the less costly group's current size, only that shortfall is called for. See "Sampling with two costs" in Details.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE or FALSE, never NA: whether to stop sampling), current_n (the total sample size), criterion_n (the sum of the two criteria), method, loss_A, cost_1, cost_2, gamma, variance_unusable (always FALSE here, because \(V_n^2\) is never below 2; carried for uniformity with the procedures whose variance estimate can be zero, negative, or not finite), and notes (a character vector, printed under the result). conf_level and width are NULL. The rule is decided group by group, so the two totals are not to be compared with each other: current_n can be at least criterion_n while one group is still short of its own criterion. In that case a note names the group. If every observation within each group is the same, or the same to ten significant digits, there is no pooled standard deviation to divide by and the standardized mean difference is not estimable: smd, risk, the two criteria, and criterion_n are NA, the rule is reported as not met, and a note says why (next_n1 and next_n2 do not depend on the estimate and are still reported). That test is relative to the size of the values, so observations that do vary but share a large common offset (each group's range is at most \(10^{-10}\) times its largest absolute value, as it can be for times recorded from a distant origin) are treated as the same too. The note then says to subtract the same constant from both groups, which leaves the standardized mean difference unchanged, and to check again. See smsd_check_methods for the print, summary, and conversion methods.

Details

The function does not collect data or keep state. Call seq_mr_smd_pilot for the starting sample sizes, collect that many observations, and call seq_mr_smd(). While attr(out, "is_satisfied") is FALSE, bring the two groups up to the sizes in the rows next_n1 and next_n2 and call it again.

The estimate is \(d = (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2)/s\), with \(s\) the pooled standard deviation (Equations 2 and 3 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2017). The article assumes a normal population with a common variance in each group; the stopping rule rests on the normal theory mean squared error of \(d\). Use seq_mr_smd_sensitivity to see what a skewed population costs. The estimate, and with it the stopping decision, is the same whatever the common units of the two groups (seconds or minutes, say), up to rounding error.

One cost for both groups. The approximate risk (their Equation 9) is $$R = A\left\{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2} + \frac{\delta^2}{2(n_1 + n_2)}\right\} + c\,(n_1 + n_2),$$ the price of the squared error plus the cost of sampling. It is smallest when each group has \(n_c = \sqrt{A/(2c)}\;\xi\) observations, with \(\xi^2 = 2 + \delta^2/4\) (their Equations 10 and 11), where it equals \(4 c\, n_c\) (their Equation 12). Because \(\delta\) is unknown, the purely sequential rule (their Equation 15) stops at the first \(n \ge m\) observations per group with $$n \ge \sqrt{\frac{A}{2c}}\left(V_n + n^{-\gamma}\right), \qquad V_n^2 = 2 + \frac{d_n^2}{4},$$ where \(m\) is the pilot size, \(V_n^2\) is their Equation 13, and \(n^{-\gamma}\) with \(0 < \gamma < 1/2\) keeps the rule from stopping too early. In the article's example (\(d\) = 1.00, \(A\) = 10,000, \(c\) = 2.40; p. 106) the rule is first met at \(n\) = 75. The article states the rule for equal group sizes. If the two groups supplied differ in size, this function uses the smaller size as \(n\), so both groups must reach the criterion.

A different cost in each group. This is the article's "A General Scenario" (pp. 106 to 107, Equations 17 to 21, with Appendix B, Equations 41 to 43). In this paragraph, subscript 1 marks the less costly group, as in the article. The approximate risk (their Equation 17) replaces the sampling cost above with \(c_1 n_1 + c_2 n_2\). Setting its derivatives to zero (their Equation 41) gives the optimal sizes: \(n_2^* = n_1^* \, r(n_1^*)\) with \(r(n) = \{1 + (c_2 - c_1) n^2 / A\}^{-1/2}\) (their Equations 19 and 43), and \(n_1^*\) solves $$n_1^* = \sqrt{\frac{A}{c_1}} \left\{1 + \frac{\delta^2}{2\,\{1 + r(n_1^*)\}^2}\right\}^{1/2}.$$ The sequential procedure samples the less costly group one observation (or batch) at a time, keeps the costlier group at \(\lceil n_1\, r(n_1) \rceil\) observations (their Equation 21 and the Stage II text), and stops at the first \(n_1\) with $$n_1 \ge \sqrt{\frac{A}{c_1}}\left[ \left\{1 + \frac{d^2}{2\,\{1 + r(n_1)\}^2}\right\}^{1/2} + n_1^{-\gamma}\right],$$ where \(d\) is computed from all observations in both groups.

Where the function departs from the article as printed.

  1. Equations 18 and 42, and the stopping rule built on them, are printed with \(\{1 + r(n_1)\}\) to the first power. The first order conditions in Equation 41 give the second power shown above. Only the second power minimizes the risk in Equation 17, and only it reduces to Equation 10 when the costs are equal (as Lemma 6 of the article states). The function uses the second power. For \(A\) = 50,000, costs of 2 and 8, and \(\delta\) = 1, the printed form gives \(n_1^*\) = 183.4; direct minimization of Equation 17 gives 175.7, which is what the form above gives.

  2. The article's two cost procedure does not reduce to its one cost procedure when \(c_1 = c_2\): its pilot (Equation 20) uses \(A/c_1\) where Equation 14 uses \(A/(2c)\), and its correction term is \(\sqrt{A/c_1}\,n^{-\gamma}\) where Equation 15 has \(\sqrt{A/(2c)}\,n^{-\gamma}\). The function uses the one cost procedure whenever the two costs supplied are equal (so c = c(3, 3) and c = 3 give identical results) and the two cost procedure whenever they differ. A small difference between the costs therefore moves the criterion by a visible amount; this is a property of the article's two procedures, not of the software. So that rounding error cannot make that choice, two costs whose relative difference is at most the square root of machine precision (about 1.5e-8) count as equal, and the smaller of the two is used: c = c(24 * 0.1, 2.4) gives the same result as c = 2.4.

  3. The article assumes the first group is the less costly one. The function applies the rule with whichever group is less costly in that role, so the order of the groups does not matter.

  4. The function is given data, not a sampling plan, so it also requires the costlier group to have at least \(\lceil n_1\, r(n_1) \rceil\) observations before reporting the rule as met.

Everything else in the two cost procedure is the article's.

Sampling with two costs. The rows next_n1 and next_n2 give the size each group should have at the next check, so the article's sampling order does not have to be coded by hand: while the rule is not met, collect observations until the groups have those sizes and call seq_mr_smd() again. Starting from the pilot sizes, each such step adds one observation to the less costly group and brings the costlier group up to \(\lceil n_1\, r(n_1) \rceil\), with \(n_1\) the less costly group's new size, which is the article's procedure with one observation per stage (its Stage II, p. 107, and the steps after it). The rows are in the order of the arguments, group 1 and group 2, whichever of them is the less costly one. If the costlier group has fewer observations than the article pairs with the less costly group's current size, the rows ask for that shortfall alone (the less costly group's row equals its current size). That gives a way to check less often than after every observation: add several observations to the less costly group and call seq_mr_smd(); if the rows then ask only for the costlier group's shortfall, collect it and call again. With one cost the rows bring each group up to one more than the smaller of the two current sizes. Sampling in another order (adding to the costlier group and topping up the less costly one) oversamples: the function can then report the rule as met, because both groups are past their criteria, at a sampling cost well above the minimum.

What to expect. The article proves that the expected final sample size and the risk approach their optimal values as \(A/c\) grows; at practical sizes the agreement is approximate, and the correction term makes the procedure take somewhat more than the optimal number of observations. With one cost, this function reproduces the article's Tables 1 and 3 within Monte Carlo error. For \(A\) = 50,000, \(c\) = 1, and \(\delta = 0\), for example, the mean final sample size per group in 5,000 replications was 235.04 (the article reports 235.04; the optimal size is 223.6), and the ratio of the realized risk to the minimum risk was 1.00. With costs of 2 and 8, \(A\) = 50,000, and \(\delta = 1\), the mean final sizes were 189.2 and 82.7 against optimal sizes of 175.7 and 81.0, and the risk ratio was 0.99 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.01). At smaller sample sizes the excess is larger: for \(A\) = 1,000,000, \(c\) = 500, and \(\delta = 0\) the mean final size was 50.0 against an optimal 44.7, as in the article's Table 3.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with sequential estimation. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113. doi:10.1037/met0000089

See also

seq_mr_smd_pilot for the pilot sizes and seq_mr_smd_sensitivity to study the procedure before collecting data; the accuracy in parameter estimation companion seq_aipe_smd; in DMAR, mr_smd (the one cost procedure, from summary statistics), the estimator smd, and the fixed sample size planner ss_aipe_smd.

Other seq_mr_smd: seq_mr_sensitivity, seq_mr_smd_pilot()

Author

Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in, Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# The pilot data of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017, p. 105): reading
# scores of children with high and low exposure to same language
# subtitling. Assessing one child costs 2.40 dollars; A = 2500 / 0.5^2.
high_sls <- c(11, 7, 22, 13, 6, 9, 11, 16, 12, 17, 14, 8, 16)
low_sls  <- c(3, 6, 10, 8, 14, 5, 12, 10, 6, 8, 13, 5, 9)
seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 10000, c = 2.40)
#> [1] 13
seq_mr_smd(high_sls, low_sls, A = 10000, c = 2.40)
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (standardized mean difference))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 26
#>   Criterion n     : 164
#> 
#>   smd               : 1.021484
#>   risk              : 1801.521
#>   mean_1            : 12.46154
#>   mean_2            : 8.384615
#>   optimal_n1        : 82
#>   optimal_n2        : 82
#>   current_n1        : 13
#>   current_n2        : 13
#>   next_n1           : 14
#>   next_n2           : 14
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Two costs: a visit to a child in the second group costs twice as much.
# While the rule is not met, bring each group up to the size in its
# next_n row and check again. The rows follow the article's sampling
# order whichever group is the costlier one, so the loop also runs as
# written with cost <- c(6, 3).
set.seed(113)
A <- 2000
cost <- c(3, 6)                  # group 1, group 2
true_mean <- c(0.5, 0)
m <- seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = A, c = cost)
y <- list(rnorm(m[["group_1"]], mean = true_mean[1]),
          rnorm(m[["group_2"]], mean = true_mean[2]))
check <- seq_mr_smd(y[[1]], y[[2]], A = A, c = cost)
while (!attr(check, "is_satisfied")) {
  next_n <- check$value[check$term %in% c("next_n1", "next_n2")]
  for (j in 1:2) {
    y[[j]] <- c(y[[j]],
                rnorm(next_n[j] - length(y[[j]]), mean = true_mean[j]))
  }
  check <- seq_mr_smd(y[[1]], y[[2]], A = A, c = cost)
}
check
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (standardized mean difference))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 51
#>   Criterion n     : 51
#> 
#>   smd               : 0.2240416
#>   risk              : 378.5003
#>   mean_1            : 0.5786443
#>   mean_2            : 0.3443293
#>   optimal_n1        : 31
#>   optimal_n2        : 20
#>   current_n1        : 31
#>   current_n2        : 20
#>   next_n1           : 31
#>   next_n2           : 20
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
